BXL-2425-00022-v4.headline: Call on the Brussels government to press Belgium to get food and humanitarian aid into Gaza — by air drops if the land routes stay blocked.
BXL-2425-00022-v4.proposed_by: Ilyas Mouani (Vooruit.brussels) as lead author; co-signed by Zakia Khattabi (Ecolo), Fouad Ahidar (Team Fouad Ahidar) and others across several groups; rapporteurs Zakia Khattabi (Ecolo) and Ismail Luahabi (MR)
BXL-2425-00022-v4.source_brief:
Since 2 March 2025, no food or humanitarian aid has entered Gaza; the World Food Programme reported on 16 May that the emergency had never been greater, with half a million people — one in five — facing famine. This resolution asks the Brussels government to lobby the federal government to put urgent humanitarian aid to Gaza on the EU Foreign Affairs and Humanitarian Aid Ministers' agenda, and to call on the European Commission to enable aid delivery. An amendment sought to replace explicit references to air drops with humanitarian land corridors; supporters of the original text rejected it; the amendment was voted down, and the unamended text was then put to a final vote.

- **What it asks:** the Brussels government to relay a request up the chain — to the federal government, then to the EU — for guaranteed, unblocked access to Gaza for food and humanitarian aid.
- **The air-drop dispute:** supporters argued air drops are the last remaining route given the blockade; opponents countered that air drops are technically dangerous, require Israeli permission, and that land convoys already waiting at the border are the right mechanism.
- **The competence objection:** several groups repeatedly noted that foreign-policy levers belong to the federal level, not a regional parliament, and that three Brussels resolutions on Gaza in three months created false expectations among citizens.
- **The rub:** whether a regional parliament's symbolic signal amplifies international pressure and reflects its Palestinian diaspora's concerns, or whether it oversteps competence, polarises Brussels society, and delivers no practical change.
deep_facts: The text is a proposition de résolution (dossier NRS. A-122/1 and 2 — 2024/2025) tabled by Ilyas Mouani (Vooruit.brussels) and examined under urgency; it passed committee unanimously before the plenary session (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

Since 2 March 2025 no food or humanitarian aid had entered Gaza; on the day of the debate, Israel's plan to demolish remaining infrastructure in Gaza was entering into force; the World Food Programme declared the emergency had never been so acute (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

An IPC report dated 12 May 2025, cited by PS speaker Nadia El Yousfi, stated that the entire population of Gaza faced acute food insecurity; some 500,000 people — one in five — were at risk of famine (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

In March 2024 the Belgian B-FAST cell, under then-Defence Minister Ludivine Dedonder (PS), had air-dropped 164 tonnes of humanitarian material over Gaza; speakers noted nothing comparable had occurred in the fifteen months since (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

The Brussels Parliament had already adopted a resolution on 14 February 2025 calling for an arms export ban to Israel, a halt to subsidies to complicit companies and for sanctions; several speakers, notably PTB's Patricia Parga Vega, argued the federal parties present had done nothing to implement those measures at federal level (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

Fouad Ahidar (Team Fouad Ahidar) stated he had visited Gaza eight times, most recently accompanying two trucks of supplies for which he was asked to pay 300 dollars per truck at the Egyptian border, despite thousands of trucks already waiting; he counted 15,000 children killed since 7 October 2023 (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

MR's Ismail Luahabi filed amendment no. 1 to replace references to air drops with 'humanitarian corridors' and to widen 'aide alimentaire' to 'aide humanitaire' covering medicines and clothing; he noted that air drops require Israel's explicit permission, that a single military aircraft carries 15 tonnes requiring 120 daily flights, and that drops had previously killed or injured people (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

Ecolo's Zakia Khattabi responded that she found it 'indigne' for MR to express concern about the danger of food drops while never having condemned the dropping of bombs on Gaza (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

Gilles Verstraeten (N-VA) supported the MR amendment on practical grounds — preferring land convoys as the primary mechanism — but said N-VA's support for the resolution was not conditional on the amendment's adoption (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).

The federal Arizona coalition government (including MR, Les Engagés, cd&v, N-VA and Vooruit) had tabled a federal resolution on Gaza the previous day (15 May 2025), prompting some parties to argue the Brussels text was partly superseded (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 21).
BXL-2425-00022-v4.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The amendment battle over 'air drops vs. land corridors' is the visible debate but the deeper tension is procedural: the MR used a technical objection (dangers of drops, Israeli veto on airspace) to reframe the request in terms more palatable to a government that is simultaneously negotiating the federal resolution — a way to back the text without endorsing its most confrontational framing.
- The timing — tabling the Brussels resolution the day after Vooruit abstained from the Gaza committee at the federal Parliament — gave PTB and left groups political ammunition to accuse proposers of symbolic gesture-politics while blocking concrete action at the level where it would actually matter.
- A wide final consensus, if it emerges once the amendment falls, would obscure significant disagreement on the resolution's underlying logic: parties that thought it outside Brussels competence or symbolically insufficient still voted yes rather than split the plenary just before a sensitive second vote on the ICC.
- For a regional parliament without foreign-policy competence, the vote's main function is reputational signalling toward Brussels's large Palestinian diaspora and toward EU-level actors, rather than any operational effect on aid delivery.
BXL-2425-00022-v4.raw_fr: La proposition de résolution demande au gouvernement de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale d'intervenir auprès du gouvernement fédéral pour qu'il agisse au niveau de l'Union européenne afin de garantir l'acheminement urgent d'aide alimentaire et humanitaire à Gaza, notamment en inscrivant ce point à l'ordre du jour des ministres européens compétents. Un amendement, rejeté en séance, visait à remplacer la référence aux largages aériens par celle aux couloirs humanitaires terrestres et à élargir la notion d'aide alimentaire à l'aide humanitaire au sens large. Le texte originel a ensuite été adopté lors du vote final.

BXL-2425-00022-v5.headline: Demand that Belgium arrest anyone wanted by the International Criminal Court who sets foot on Belgian soil — including those wanted over the war in Gaza.
BXL-2425-00022-v5.proposed_by: Jamal Ikazban (PS) as first signatory, and co-signers including Nadia El Yousfi (PS) and others across left and centrist groups; rapporteur Nadia El Yousfi (PS); dossier NOS A-114/1, 2 and 3 — 2024/2025
BXL-2425-00022-v5.source_brief:
This resolution was triggered by remarks made by Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever in April 2025, which were widely understood as signalling reluctance to execute a potential ICC arrest warrant, notably against Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu. The text asks the Brussels Parliament to call on Belgium to respect its international legal commitments, specifically the Rome Statute obligation to arrest and transfer persons subject to ICC warrants. By the time of the final vote, the federal government had issued clarifications — through the Foreign Affairs and Justice ministers and a federal resolution — affirming Belgium's commitment to international law.

- **Why a Brussels vote?** Supporters argued the Prime Minister's remarks created genuine doubt about Belgium's rule-of-law reliability; they saw a regional signal as necessary and timely given pressure on the ICC from the US and Hungary's withdrawal.
- **The selective-justice charge:** critics argued the text named only Israel-related mandates and omitted warrants against Vladimir Putin, Omar al-Bashir and others, questioning whether it reflected genuine universalism or political targeting.
- **The competence and timing defence:** other groups contended that since the federal government and prime minister had already clarified their position, the resolution had no further object; execution of ICC warrants is a judicial, not executive, matter.
- **The rub:** whether reaffirming international-law obligations is a legitimate act of regional parliamentary expression or an out-of-competence move that imports geopolitical conflict into Brussels's social fabric.
deep_facts: The text is a proposition de résolution (dossier NOS A-114/1, 2 and 3 — 2024/2025) with PS as first signatory; it was tabled as a matter of urgency following statements by Prime Minister De Wever that were interpreted as signalling possible non-compliance with ICC arrest warrants (CRI, 16 May 2025 — sessions nr. 21 and nr. 22).

Prime Minister De Wever had stated publicly that executing a possible ICC warrant against Netanyahu would not be straightforward, citing a scenario in which the Israeli PM might make an emergency landing in Belgium; N-VA's Gilles Verstraeten characterised the remarks as 'excessive intellectual honesty' from De Wever's earlier role as party chairman, inappropriate for a sitting premier (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

Federal Foreign Affairs Minister Maxime Prévot and Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden issued clarifications in early April 2025 stating that the remarks had not been discussed in government and that Belgium would continue to support the ICC and execute its decisions; on 9 April, Verlinden confirmed before the Chamber that Belgium, as a Rome Statute party, is legally obliged to execute ICC arrest and transfer requests (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

The federal Arizona coalition majority had, as of 12 May 2025, tabled a resolution in the Chamber reaffirming Belgium's support for the ICC and the execution of its decisions including arrest warrants; Les Engagés and N-VA cited this to argue the Brussels resolution was without object (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

PS's Jamal Ikazban added new urgency to the debate by reporting that ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan had lost access to his email (Microsoft had suspended his account), that his bank accounts had been frozen, and that American ICC officials had been warned they risked arrest if they set foot in the United States — all in connection with the indictment of Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

MR's Clémentine Barzin argued the text was selective: it referenced Mohammed Deif (who had died) but did not characterise the 7 October attacks as terrorist, and made no mention of existing ICC warrants against Vladimir Putin (Ukraine war) or Omar al-Bashir (Darfur), among others (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

Barzin also warned against importing the conflict into Brussels society, citing Unia data linking the rise of antisemitism in Brussels directly to the Gaza war, and argued the repeated passage of resolutions outside Brussels competence was damaging institutional credibility (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

Ecolo's Farida Tahar and Groen's Celia Groothedde argued that the rule-of-law concern was locally relevant: Groothedde noted that the 'Free Gaza' inscriptions visible across Brussels reflected a feeling among communities of colour that their lives were treated as less valuable, making this an issue for Brussels residents as well as an international one (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

DéFI's Joëlle Maison announced a personal abstention on the grounds that the resolution had lost its primary object following the federal clarifications, while colleagues Jonathan de Patoul and Cécile Jodogne voted in favour (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).

Open Vld's Imane Belguenani explained that her group had maintained a twenty-year practice of abstaining on international-affairs resolutions at Brussels level, but had made an exception for the previous A-122 vote 'to avoid breaking consensus' (CRI, 16 May 2025 — session nr. 22).
BXL-2425-00022-v5.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The resolution was essentially written into futility between drafting and vote: within days of tabling, the federal government's own clarifications removed the main factual premise, leaving PS to argue the value of belt-and-suspenders symbolic reaffirmation against parties that could plausibly reply 'the problem is already solved'.
- The 'selective justice' charge (Putin missing from the text) is MR's strongest analytical point and hardest for supporters to rebut: a text framed as universal but operationally specific to one conflict opens itself to the accusation that international law is being deployed as a political instrument rather than a principle.
- The separation-of-powers argument (execution of warrants is judicial, not executive) is constitutionally correct and provides a face-saving rationale for MR and cd&v to oppose or abstain without appearing to endorse non-compliance with the ICC — their objection is procedural, not substantive.
- The Unia data on rising antisemitism gives MR an additional local-competence hook: social cohesion is a genuine Brussels competence, so opposing the resolution on those grounds recasts a foreign-policy dispute as a legitimate regional governance concern.
BXL-2425-00022-v5.raw_fr: La proposition de résolution demande à la Belgique de respecter ses engagements internationaux en matière de justice pénale, notamment l'exécution des mandats d'arrêt émis par la Cour pénale internationale. Déposé en urgence à la suite de déclarations du Premier ministre De Wever interprétées comme remettant en cause ces obligations, le texte a été débattu alors que le gouvernement fédéral avait entre-temps clarifiés sa position par la voix des ministres des Affaires étrangères et de la Justice, ainsi que par le dépôt d'une résolution fédérale réaffirmant le soutien de la Belgique à la CPI.
